original_text: Write a story from a perspective of a man. Include some conversation in the story. Avoid using the letter i more than twice.
text: Write a story from a man's perspective. Include some conversation. Avoid using the letter i more than twice.
original_raw_output:
Morning sun leaked through the blinds, sketching pale bars across the hardwood floor. I stood there in socks, mug warming both hands, listening to the old refrigerator hum like it had something hopeful to say. Today would be ordinary, or so the calendar claimed. But the letter on the table—stiff paper, blue ink—said the opposite.

“Are you going to open it?” Mara leaned in the doorway, one sock yellow, one gray. She always did that, as though mischief started at the toes.

“Eventually,” came out before any plan formed. Steam rose from the mug, soft ghost, drifting toward the ceiling where a crack wandered like a lazy river.

She crossed the kitchen, tugged the chair with a scrape, sat. “You’ve been ‘eventually’-ing that envelope for three days.”

“Four,” I admitted, and that was one of the two slips. The letter stared up with the sort of patience that can make a person feel small. Across from me, Mara sipped from her chipped cup. Red fox painted on it, tail curled. It had survived three apartments, two storms, and one move undertaken at midnight with a borrowed truck that coughed smoke like a stage actor.

“You remember Dad’s map?” she asked.

A nod. A foldout atlas, edges soft as bread, roads spidering through states named like promises.

“He used to say a route never shows what you’ll actually meet. Only where you might end up.” She drummed fingers on the table. “Open the map.”

I smiled. She always translated life into our father’s sayings. “How about you do the honors?” The envelope slid her way.

She pulled the letter free, unfolded it carefully, as though it might bruise. Eyes scanned lines, left to right, then back. A pause. The fox cup met the table with a gentle knock.

“Well?” My voice sounded like someone else’s—frayed, hopeful, wary.

“It’s from the lighthouse board,” she said. “They approved your proposal. The grant. The restoration.” Her grin arrived late, as if it had run the whole block to get here. “You got it.”

The room tilted, not in a bad way. That lighthouse—stone tower on the northern cape, windows clouded with salt, stairs spiraling like a quiet scream—had lived in dreams for months. “So they’ll let me bring it back,” I said, and there went the second slip. No more uses left, then. Every other sentence needed trimming, a careful step around the forbidden letter.

Mara laughed, wiped at one eye with her wrist. “They’ll let you bring it back,” she echoed. “About time someone did.”

Memories woke: a summer afternoon at the cape, both of us racing gulls, pockets clinking with shells. The old keeper had let us climb to the lamp. Wind pressed at the glass like a curious hand. The sea stretched out forever, not blue so much as metal warmed by sun.

Now, the grant meant scaffolds, paint, a new lens. A small crew. A larger promise.

“Go see it,” Mara said, as though she read minds. “Today.”

“Work,” I began, but the word lay there, thin as paper. The office could spare a day. No, two. The calendar made room when the heart insisted.

She folded the letter, tucked it back. “Leave the map to me,” she said, popping up, grabbing keys off the hook. On the way out, she tapped the fridge. “Keep humming, old friend.”

We drove north under a sky poured from pewter. The radio threw out a half-remembered song about roads and rain. Cornfields gave way to slopes and marsh, then to scrub and rock. The ocean arrived all at once, a continuous jawline, teeth made of foam.

The lighthouse lifted from the headland exactly as memory arranged it—stubborn, weather-chewed, still standing. Crosswinds shoved shoulders. We leaned into them, both of us laughing. The wood door stuck, then let go with a sigh.

Inside, the air smelled of salt, dust, old rope. Steps spiraled up, narrow and steep. Boots tapped rhythm. At each landing, a slit of a window offered a sideways glance at the world: gulls stitching gray sky, a trawler crawling toward harbor, a boy in a red jacket throwing a stick, a dog flinging itself after.

“Dad would haunt us for taking so long,” Mara joked, pausing to catch breath.

“Dad would refuse to haunt a place with this many stairs,” came my answer. That surprised a snort from her.

At the top, glass framed the sea like a painting no museum could hang. The lamp—dull brass, lens cracked—rested under a shawl of cobwebs. Sea roar filled the space, soft thunder repeating itself.

Mara set her palms on the rim of the housing. “Imagine this turning again,” she said, voice gone reverent. “Night boats seeing home.”

Home. That word dropped anchor somewhere behind ribs. The grant would buy parts, yes, but more than that: it would buy a beacon for strangers, a steady hand for storms.

A shuffle stirred downstairs. Footsteps. A figure rose through the hatch, cap in hand. Broad shoulders, beard like a storm cloud. “Thought I heard folks,” he said, the accent old harbor. “Name’s Everett. Been watching over the place since your dad left. Well—watching the lack of watching, you could say.”

Mara stuck out a hand. “Mara. This is my brother.”

Everett’s grip held warmth and sandpaper. “Saw your application. Good words,” he said, nodding, only an eyelid betraying surprise that words could move stones. “You two back to set this beacon right?”

“That’s the dream,” I said, sidestepping the dangerous vowel by keeping the sentence lean.

Everett dug in his jacket, produced a ring of keys heavy as history. “Then these are yours. For now, for work.” He dangled them, metal winking. “Careful with the gallery glass. Last storm tried to take it. Lost a pane. The sea enjoys theft.”

“We’ll treat it like a cathedral,” Mara promised.

Everett chuckled. “Cathedral to fog, maybe. Sound carries out here, but not much carries back. Keep that in mind once the lamp burns.” He looked over the rail at waves. “A lot of lost souls rely on light they’ll never meet.”

He left then, boots receding into the tower’s throat. Silence returned, except for wind and water and a loose hinge singing its small note.

Mara spun one key on her finger. “So,” she said. “You’ll need help. Volunteers. Permits. A list taller than this tower.”

“Start with windows,” I suggested. “Let the room see out.”

We went down and walked around the base, hands on stone. Lichen mapped creams and greens like the skin of old apples. A gull stood on the railing, eye bright, head cocked as though judging our worthiness.

“Okay, judge,” Mara said. “We’ll see you at dawn with rags.”

On the drive back, dusk painted the world in bruised lavender. Houses winked on, one square at a time. Mara turned down the radio.

“Remember that storm?” she asked. “The one that cut power for two days? You told me a story about a ship made of bread. I asked how bread could sail. You said the ocean was soup.”

“Soup supports bread,” I said, and we both laughed, because the logic had the stubbornness of childhood. Those days, Dad kept candles in bottles and never let us be afraid of dark. He said night was just the long breath before morning spoke.

At home, the envelope lay where we left it, lighter now, as though worry weighed more than paper. The fridge hummed approval. I sat with the map, traced Route 7 north, then the local road to the cape, the small drawn star from our childhood still penciled in at the headland. Mara wrote Notes on a pad: glass, paint, lens, harness, crew, permits. At the bottom she added: soup for the crew, because of course she would.

Phone buzzed. A message from Everett: Tomorrow looks clear. Tides low at noon. Bring gloves. Bring heart.

Mara read over my shoulder. “Bring heart,” she said, and placed a hand over her chest, then over mine. “Check.”

Night came soft. Outside, a neighbor walked a dog that refused to hurry. Across the street, someone practiced a trumpet—hesitant scales, then a phrase that almost found a song. I stood at the window, watched the dark settle, felt in it not a swallow, but an opening.

Through the house moved a list of things to do and buy, a carousel of tasks. Under all that, a steadier current. A tower on a cliff. A light that would return after long absence. Boats out there would see a pulse and alter course. Some captain would exhale. A child would press a nose to glass and name a blinking star on earth.

Mara flicked off the kitchen light. “Tomorrow,” she said.

“Tomorrow,” I answered.

In bed, the old spring squeaked a small protest, then rested. The city slept in sections. A siren skirted the edge of things and slid away. Breath slowed. The mind arranged tools on an imaginary table: wrenches, rags, hope, salt, patience. Somewhere between awake and under, the lamp above the sea turned once, then again, though no hand had yet set it moving.

Storm rolled over the old boathouse as dusk sank into the harbor. Nets hung like tired cobwebs, and gulls cackled from the pilings. I stood on the warped planks, hands deep in a coat pocket, waiting for Marco. He always came late when thunder promised trouble.

He showed, shoes slapping puddles, curly hair plastered to his forehead. “You look older every season,” he said, breath showing white.

“Storms carry mirrors,” he added, grinning, and leaned under the awning. “Got the key?”

“Yeah.” I handed it over. “You sure about this?”

“Sure as salt.” He jiggled the lock. Wood groaned. The door swung wide, and the smell of oil and old rope shoved out into the rainy air.

We stepped inside, lanterns hemming a little world of rust and dust. The skiff lay keel-up, ribs exposed like a patient on a table. “Last boat your father ever trusted,” Marco said. “He’d have told us to set her right.”

“He’d have told us to go home before the sky split,” I said.

Marco laughed. “He’d have said both.”

He knelt with a chisel, and the steel kissed a stubborn nail. Thunder climbed the roof, shaking it. We worked without talk for a bit, the rhythm of tapping and prying like an odd old song we both knew. When the rain really started, it fell loud enough to cancel the world.

“Remember that summer we stole cherries from Rosario?” Marco asked. “He chased us with a broom.”

“He swung like a man trying to swat fog,” I said. “You tripped over your own feet and took me down with you.”

“You twisted your ankle. Still won, though.” He smirked. “We escaped with three cherries and a lecture.”

“Best three in history.”

A lull came with the work. The boathouse breathed that slow, damp breath old buildings learn from their owners. Outside, a siren moaned and faded. My hands found the grain of the skiff, smooth as bone.

Marco stopped, glanced over. “You gonna tell her?”

“What makes you think there’s a her?”

“Your coat says so,” he said, nodding at the folded paper peeking from the inside pocket. “Only letters make men iron their collars.”

“Wasn’t going to,” I said. “Not yet.”

“Because you’re scared.”

“Because I know storms.” The words came out soft and heavy. “They start with a bit of wind, end with roofs in trees.”

He blew dust off the chisel. “You always talk like a map. Lines, warnings, tiny boats near monsters. Maybe she reads maps, though.”

“Maybe.”

We went back to the skiff. The lantern flame jittered at each thunderclap. Water tapped its way through a roof knot and fell, steady, into a bucket. Drip, drip, drip. The old heartbeat of the place.

“Your father left you more than this heap,” Marco said after a while. “He left you stubbornness, a decent backhand, and a habit of staring at the horizon like it owes you rent.”

“He left me a boathouse with a thousand leaks.”

Marco grinned. “He left you a reason to fix them.”

Rain shifted, grew lighter. Gulls sounded less like arguments and more like gossip. Marco’s chisel found one last nail, and the skiff’s plank gave with a sigh, a kind of relief.

“All right,” he said, rubbing his hands. “She’ll float again.” He looked at me. “You gonna float, too?”

“Tomorrow, maybe.”

“Tonight’s better.” He pointed with his chin at the coat pocket. “Go on. Tell her you’re not a storm. Tell her you’re a harbor.”

“Harbors flood.”

“So do hearts. People still dock.”

We laughed, both of us a little embarrassed by the corny note. The lantern sputtered, almost went out, then caught. Marco closed the toolbox and stood. “I’ll lock up,” he said. “You walk. If you change your mind, come back, and we’ll pretend we lost the key.”

He left with a slap of wet footsteps and a hum of some song from when we were kids, something about summer and a radio that never quite tuned right. The boathouse settled. The letter weighed a ton in my pocket, then nothing, then too much again.

I took it out. Paper had the soft edge of something carried too long. Her name looked brave at the top; my words underneath did not. But there they were: plain, honest, no grand choir. I folded the paper, slid it back, and stepped into the rinsed night.

Streetlights hung halos on the flooded street. The storm had spent itself, leaving the harbor breathing and shiny. I walked past Rosario’s market, closed now, the shade pulled, a broom leaning like a guard asleep at his post. Past the diner where new coffee was always five minutes away and the floor squeaked in exactly one place. Past the bench where my father used to wait for tide and time.

When I reached her building, a cat watched from a windowsill, green eyes clever. I put a hand on the buzzer, pulled it back, put it there again. The door clicked; someone was leaving. A woman in a red scarf smiled small and vanished into the wet. I slipped inside before the door sighed shut.

Stairs smelled like lemons and old paint. On the second floor, I knocked and heard footsteps, then her voice asking, “Who is it?”

“Me,” I said, and hated how small that sounded.

The door opened. She wore a sweater the color of the sea when it pretends to be calm. “You’re soaked,” she said, and then, softer, “You came.”

“I came,” I said. One of two. The rules in my head clanked. She stood aside and I crossed the threshold.

In her warm apartment, a kettle began to sing. She moved to grab it, glancing back. “Well?”

I took the letter from the pocket and held it out, an offering and a surrender. “Read after tea?”

She tilted her head, smiled the way people smile when they know the shape of what’s coming, even if not the words. “After tea,” she said.

She poured, steam curling like friendly ghosts. Cups clicked, soft. Outside, water dripped from roofs into gutters and from gutters into earth, and somewhere behind the sound, a boat remembered water, a man remembered courage, and the storm, having spent its voice, listened.

How to Train Your Dog: A Kid-Friendly Guide

Training your dog can be fun, rewarding, and a great way to build a strong friendship. With a little patience and a lot of love, you’ll teach your pup cool skills and good manners. Ready for the adventure? Let’s go!

Before You Start
- Ask a grown-up for help and permission.
- Keep training sessions short—5 to 10 minutes is best.
- Gather tiny, yummy treats your dog loves.
- Pick a quiet place with fewer distractions.

Training Tips for Success
- Be positive: Reward what you like, ignore or redirect what you don’t.
- Be patient: Dogs learn at different speeds.
- Be consistent: Use the same words and hand signals every time.

Teach the Basics

1) Name Game
- Say your dog’s name in a happy voice.
- When they look at you, say “Yes!” and give a treat.
- Repeat a few times each day so they learn that looking at you is awesome.

2) Sit
- Hold a treat close to your dog’s nose.
- Slowly move it up and back over their head.
- As their bottom touches the ground, say “Sit,” then “Yes!” and give a treat.
- Practice in different rooms for less confusion.

3) Down
- Ask for “Sit” first.
- Move a treat from their nose straight down to the floor, then out a little.
- When they lie down, say “Down,” then “Yes!” and reward.

4) Come
- Clip on a lightweight leash in a safe space.
- Crouch down, open your arms, and cheerfully say “Come!”
- When your dog reaches you, celebrate with treats and praise.
- Make coming to you the best thing ever so they’ll choose you over distractions.

5) Leave It
- Place a treat in your closed fist.
- Let your dog sniff. When they back off, say “Yes!” and give a different treat from your other hand.
- This teaches them that ignoring temptation brings a better reward.

Good Manners

- No jumping: If your dog jumps, turn your body away and look up. When all four paws are on the floor, say “Yes!” and reward. Dogs repeat what works!
- Gentle mouths: If teeth touch skin during play, stop the game for a moment. Calmly restart when they’re gentle.
- Leash walking: Hold a treat by your leg and take a step. If your dog stays by you, say “Yes!” and treat. Take a few more steps. Keep it short and happy.

Make Training a Game

- Treasure hunt: Hide a few treats around one room and let your dog “Find it!”
- Trick time: Try “Spin,” “High five,” or “Touch” (nose to your hand). Tricks build focus and are great brain workouts.
- Puzzle toys: These keep your dog busy and help them learn to solve problems.

Safety First

- Always be kind. Never yell or hit—scary training makes learning harder.
- Ask before approaching other dogs.
- Put away chew toys you don’t want shared, and keep training in safe spaces.

How to Fix Common Hiccups

- Not listening? Make it easier: train in a quieter place, use tastier treats, or ask for a simpler behavior.
- Too wiggly? Do a few “Sits” and “Downs” to help them settle. Keep sessions shorter, not longer.
- Boredom? Mix in tricks and play. If your dog is having less fun, take a quick break.

Your Daily Plan

- Morning: 5 minutes of basics (Sit, Down, Come).
- Afternoon: Short walk with “loose-leash” practice.
- Evening: One fun trick and a tiny treasure hunt.

Celebrate the Finale

At the end of the week, show your family what your dog can do—this is your training finale! Make a mini show with “Sit,” “Down,” “Come,” and a favorite trick. Give your dog extra praise and a special treat. You did this together!

Remember

- Short, happy sessions work best.
- Reward the behavior you want.
- Practice a little every day.
- Training is about teamwork and trust.

High fives to you and tail wags to your pup—now go have fun learning together!

2) Sit

- When elbows touch the floor, “Yes!” and treat.
- Keep movements slow and smooth.

4) Come
- Start indoors on a leash or short distance.
- Crouch, open your arms, and say “Come!” in a happy voice.
- When the dog runs to you, “Yes!”, treat, and celebrate.
- Never call to scold—coming should always mean something good.

5) Stay
- Ask for “Sit.” Hold your hand out like a stop sign and say “Stay.”
- Count “one,” then “Yes!” and treat.
- Gradually add seconds and take tiny steps back. If they move, reset calmly and try a shorter stay.

6) Leave It
- Hold a treat in a closed fist. Let your dog sniff. When they back off, say “Yes!” and give a different treat from the other hand.
- Add the words “Leave it.” This helps with manners around food, toys, and things outside.

- Shake/Paw: Hold a treat in your fist. Most dogs paw at your hand—mark and reward. Add “Paw” as they get it.
- Spin: Lure your dog in a small circle with a treat; say “Spin” once they follow easily.
- Touch: Present your hand like a target. When the dog boops it with their nose, mark and treat. Great for guiding politely.

Leash Walks Made Easy
- Start in the yard or indoors. Reward your dog for walking by your side and checking in with you.
- If they pull, stop and wait for slack in the leash, then move forward. Pulling less gets them where they want to go faster—dogs learn that quickly.

Good Habits for Everyday Life
- Mealtime Manners: Ask for “Sit” before putting the bowl down.
- Doorway Pause: “Sit” and “Stay” before going outside—then “Okay!” to release.
- Calm Greetings: Teach “Sit” for attention; jumping gets less attention, sitting gets pets and praise.

Keeping It Fun
- Mix rewards: tiny treats, praise, toys, or a quick game of fetch.
- Celebrate small wins and end sessions on a success.
- If something isn’t working, make it easier and try again.

Common Bumps and Quick Fixes
- Dog is distracted: Train in a quieter spot or use a tastier treat.
- Dog won’t listen: Shorten sessions and ask for simpler behaviors first.
- Dog seems shy or worried: Use softer voices, more distance, and extra praise.

The Finale: A Mini Talent Show
After a few weeks, host a family dog show! Put together a routine: Name Game, Sit, Down, Spin, Paw, and a cheerful “Come” to end. Kids can make a simple poster, choose music, and announce each trick. It’s a fun way to show progress and build confidence.

A Note for Parents
- Supervise, set up the environment for success, and help with timing and consistency.
- Keep training positive—no punishment. Rewarding the behaviors you like leads to less frustration and faster learning.
- If challenges persist (fear, reactivity, guarding), consult a certified force-free trainer.

With patience, play, and practice, your child and dog will grow into a fantastic team. Start small, keep it kind, and enjoy the journey to your grand training finale!

1) I scale infinitely when the PM nods, but cry O(n²) during sprint planning. I’m promised to be “trivially parallelizable,” yet I deadlock in standups. I’m the architect’s vision and the intern’s nightmare. What am I?

2) I whisper “just one minor refactor,” then drag you into a 14-file diff with three migrations and a new lint rule. I’m discovered after “quickly wiring up the API.” I smell of legacy but wear a hoodie that says “microservice.” What am I?

3) I am immutable until Friday, then mutable until Monday. I live in Git, die in prod, and respawn as a hotfix. You can’t see me, yet your career depends on me. What am I?

4) You build me with layers, but I’m never a cake. Sometimes I ship with ports, other times I sink with them. I’m light by name, heavy by pull. I was supposed to save us all. What am I?

5) I am zero-cost at runtime and infinite-cost in meetings. I can be generalized into oblivion, or specialized into résumé bullets. I give you power, type safety, and occasional existential dread. What am I?

6) I run everywhere except on your machine. I am “cross-platform” provided you never leave the CI container. I have flexible configuration that is rigidly undocumented. I am version 3.1.4 but require 3.1.3. What am I?

7) I am always green at 2 a.m. and always red during demos. I am brittle, flaky, and opinionated, yet I claim “confidence.” I break when you change nothing and pass when you change everything. What am I?

8) I thrive on entropy and thrive despite it. I am the emergent behavior of 10 simple rules and 1 undocumented ENV variable. I teach humility, enforce no guarantees, and eat retries for breakfast. What am I?

9) I pretend to be functional, but I leak state. I pretend to be object-oriented, but I leak abstractions. I pretend to be developer-friendly, but I leak memory. I’m everyone’s favorite language until a conference talk. What am I?

10) I never forget, except when I do. I cache your joy, evict your dreams, and invalidate your assumptions. I’m the final boss hidden in plain text. What am I?

Clues swirl like logs in a distributed river. They arrive out of order, appended by timestamps, sometimes duplicated, always urgent. You grep for meaning. The Jenkins idol groans. A cron job whispers every fifteen minutes, summoning specters named “rotate” and “vacuum.” The SRE ravens caw: “Observe, observe, observe.” You expand the radius of suspicion: DNS, TLS, NTP, PTSD.

You suspect the network—a classic antagonist. “It’s always DNS,” chants the tribe. But you know the deeper lore: it’s not always DNS. Sometimes it’s timezone conversion shenanigans where yesterday meets tomorrow in a Pacific archipelago called “prod.” Sometimes it’s clock skew, or that one service whose health check says “I’m fine” while its thread pool screams in a silent heap.

You descend into the profiler’s labyrinth. CPU? Chillin’. Memory? Cozy. Locks? Socializing. You follow a trail of tiny allocations, like breadcrumbs left by a tidy Hansel. At the center: a map with a hash function that thought collisions were a myth. You patch, you pray, you deploy. The canary sings, then coughs, then negotiates with the garbage collector.

A senior engineer emerges from the mist, beard compiled with -O3. “Tell me,” they intone, “is the problem in the code, the config, or the concept?” You answer: “Yes.”

In the cafeteria of complexity, you order a plate of eventual consistency with a side of retries, seasoned by idempotency. You pour ketchup labeled “observability,” which is mostly sugar but makes everything feel traceable. You tag, you sample, you correlate. You carry context like a sacred token, passing it carefully through the function call forest, lest it be defaulted, dropped, or reinterpreted as an enum.

You remember a proverb: there are two hard things in computer science—cache invalidation, naming things, and off-by-one errors. You rename a variable and instantly become responsible for five broken dashboards and a minor philosophical debate about snake_case vs. camelCase. You fix an off-by-one and unleash a zero-based riot.

At last, the answer peeks out from behind a feature flag named “maybe.” The flag is off in staging, on in prod, and Schrödingered in your local. You flip it, and the world stabilizes. The tests turn green, the graphs smooth, the Slack grows quiet—except for a single message: “Anyone else seeing intermittent latency in the EU-West-2 canary?”

What am I?

I am the infinite jest of systems, the punchline with backpressure, the riddle of reliable software in an unreliable universe. I am your job, your joy, your doom scroll. I am complexity, pretending to be a tool. And you, dear professional, are the hero who ships anyway.

From better sleep quality and spinal relief to stress reduction and portability, hammocks offer a surprising list of benefits.

- Natural spinal alignment and pressure relief: When you lie in a properly hung hammock and position yourself diagonally across the fabric, your body distributes weight more evenly than on a flat mattress. This reduces pressure points on the shoulders, hips, and lower back. Many hammock sleepers report less morning stiffness and fewer aches. The slight cradling effect supports the natural curve of your spine, and the fabric adapts to your shape instead of forcing you to fit the surface.

- Faster sleep onset and deeper rest: The gentle rocking of a hammock can promote relaxation and help you fall asleep faster. Research on rocking motion shows it can synchronize brain waves associated with deep sleep and improve sleep continuity. Even a static hammock has a cocoon-like feel that can reduce tossing and turning, making it easier to drift off and stay asleep.

- Reduced back and joint pain for some sleepers: Side sleepers often struggle with pressure buildup on firm mattresses, while back sleepers can experience lower back strain on soft beds. A hammock, when used diagonally, supports both positions with minimal pressure points. People with mild lower back pain sometimes find relief, though anyone with chronic pain or specific spinal conditions should consult a clinician before making a switch.

- Cooler sleep and better airflow: Hammocks allow air to circulate around your body, which helps regulate temperature—especially in warm climates or stuffy rooms. For hot sleepers, this can be the difference between waking repeatedly and enjoying a full, uninterrupted night.

Here’s a clear, flexible rubric you can use to rate a teenager’s essay. Score each category from 1–5 (1 = needs major improvement, 5 = excellent). Add up for a total out of 40.

1) Thesis and Purpose
- 5: Clear, original, arguable thesis; purpose is focused throughout.
- 4: Clear thesis; mostly focused.
- 3: Thesis present but generic or partially arguable; some drift.
- 2: Vague or implied thesis; frequent drift.
- 1: No clear thesis; unclear purpose.

2) Organization and Coherence
- 5: Logical structure; strong intro/body/conclusion; smooth flow.
- 4: Clear structure; minor lapses in flow or transitions.
- 3: Basic structure; some awkward or disjointed sections.
- 2: Weak organization; difficult to follow at times.
- 1: Disorganized; very difficult to follow.

3) Development and Evidence
- 5: Ideas fully developed; specific, relevant evidence; insightful analysis.
- 4: Adequate development; generally relevant evidence; solid analysis.
- 3: Some development; evidence may be general or uneven; basic analysis.
- 2: Underdeveloped; minimal or weak evidence; limited analysis.
- 1: Little to no development; unsupported claims.

4) Explanation and Reasoning
- 5: Clear reasoning linking evidence to claims; addresses counterpoints.
- 4: Mostly clear reasoning; minor gaps; attempts counterpoints.
- 3: Reasoning present but sometimes unclear; limited counterpoint.
- 2: Frequent logical gaps; little explanation.
- 1: Largely unclear or illogical reasoning.

5) Voice and Originality
- 5: Distinct, engaging voice; original insights or perspective.
- 4: Consistent voice; some fresh ideas.
- 3: Appropriate voice; mostly conventional ideas.
- 2: Uneven or generic voice; few original elements.
- 1: Flat or inappropriate voice; no originality.

6) Language and Style
- 5: Precise word choice; varied sentence structure; appropriate tone.
- 4: Generally precise; some variety; mostly appropriate tone.
- 3: Adequate vocabulary; limited variety; tone acceptable.
- 2: Simplistic or repetitive language; awkward sentences.
- 1: Inaccurate or inappropriate language; very awkward.

7) Conventions (Grammar, Spelling, Punctuation)
- 5: Virtually error-free; errors do not distract.
- 4: Few minor errors; minimal distraction.
- 3: Some errors; occasionally distracting.
- 2: Frequent errors; often distracting.
- 1: Persistent errors; highly distracting.

8) Use of Sources (if applicable)
- 5: High-quality, relevant sources; integrated smoothly; correct citation.
- 4: Good sources; generally well integrated; mostly correct citation.
- 3: Adequate sources; mixed integration; some citation errors.
- 2: Weak or few sources; poor integration; frequent citation errors.
- 1: Little to no credible sourcing; missing citations.

Scoring Guide
- 36–40: Exceptional
- 30–35: Strong
- 24–29: Competent
- 16–23: Developing
- 8–15: Beginning

Feedback Tips
- Note one strength per category.
- Prioritize 2–3 actionable suggestions.
- Reference specific sentences or sections.
- If relevant, suggest revision steps (e.g., “clarify thesis by specifying X”).

******

Summary: Rate essays on eight categories (Thesis, Organization, Evidence, Reasoning, Voice, Style, Conventions, Sources) on a 1–5 scale, total 40. Use the scoring guide to classify overall quality and give targeted feedback with concrete examples and next steps.

3) Evidence and Development

4) Audience and Purpose Awareness

5) Style and Voice

- 30–37: Competent
- 22–29: Developing

- Did I explain how each piece of evidence supports my claim?

- Did I vary sentence structures and use precise verbs/nouns?
- Are all grammar, punctuation, and citations correct?

Then estimate your taxable income and calculate your tax using the rates for your filing status. Many people use tax software or a professional to help calculate liability, apply deductions/credits, and check whether quarterly estimated payments are needed if you’re self-employed.

Next, choose how you will file and pay. You can e-file through IRS Free File (if eligible), commercial software, or a tax professional; or you can mail paper returns, though e-file is faster and provides confirmation. To pay, options include direct debit during e-file, IRS Direct Pay from a bank account, debit/credit card (fees may apply), Electronic Federal Tax Payment System (EFTPS) for individuals and businesses, or a check with a voucher. If you can’t pay in full, request an online payment plan or consider an Offer in Compromise. Keep copies of your return and supporting documents for at least three years after you file.

In conclusion, set reminders for key deadlines (generally April 15 for individuals, with extensions available) and reconcile any withholding via your W-4 to avoid underpayment penalties. Review life changes—marriage, dependents, new jobs, side income—that affect how you calculate and file next year. Finally, monitor IRS notices in your mail or online account, respond promptly if contacted, and update your records regularly to keep the process smooth from start to conclusion. ***

original_raw_output:
Have you ever noticed how some parts of the year are hot and sunny, and other parts are cold and snowy? That’s because Earth has seasons: spring, summer, fall, and winter. Here’s why:

- Earth goes around the Sun once every year, like a big circle.
- Earth is tilted, like a spinning top leaning to the side. It’s tilted by about the amount you’d tip your head to rest it on your shoulder.
- Because of this tilt, different parts of Earth get more direct sunlight at different times of the year.

What that looks like:
- When the top half of Earth (the Northern Hemisphere) is tilted toward the Sun, it gets more direct sunlight and longer days. That’s summer there! At the same time, the bottom half (the Southern Hemisphere) is tilted away, so it gets less direct sunlight and shorter days—that’s winter there.
- About six months later, the situation flips: the Northern Hemisphere tilts away (winter) and the Southern Hemisphere tilts toward the Sun (summer).
- In between, during spring and fall, neither half is tilted strongly toward or away from the Sun, so temperatures are milder and days and nights are closer in length.

Important note:
- It’s not because we’re closer to or farther from the Sun. The tilt and how direct the sunlight is what really matters.

Quick check:
- Longer days and higher Sun in the sky = warmer (summer).
- Shorter days and lower Sun in the sky = cooler (winter).

P.S. If you stand a stick in the ground and watch its shadow at the same time each day, you’ll see the shadow get shorter in summer and longer in winter—that’s the Sun’s height changing because of Earth’s tilt!

When your part of Earth is tilted away from the Sun:
